blocks.text: **The task.** Given the start and end times of meetings, find the minimum number of rooms needed so that no two overlapping meetings share a room.

blocks.code:
input:   [[0,30], [5,10], [15,20]]
output:  2

[0,30] overlaps both others, but [5,10] and [15,20] do not
overlap each other — so two rooms suffice.

blocks.text: "Minimum rooms" sounds like an assignment problem, but it is not. The answer is simply the **maximum number of meetings running at the same time** — the peak of the running count.
If three meetings ever overlap, you need three rooms; if that never happens, you never need a third. So the question becomes: what is the highest the active count ever reaches?
`a[1] - b[1]` puts the `-1` first when times are equal. So a meeting ending at 10 frees its room before a meeting starting at 10 claims one — they share a room rather than needing two.
That matches how rooms actually work. If your problem says back-to-back bookings need separate rooms, reverse the tie-break.
**Time: O(N log N)** for sorting 2N events. **Space: O(N)** for the event list.
This same sweep answers a whole family: peak server load, maximum simultaneous downloads, busiest hour. Once you see intervals as +1/−1 events, they all reduce to the same running total.
